summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 as published in the Official Journal

text.en: The EU's main economic and financial sanctions against Russia over its war on Ukraine: bans on trade in many goods and services, restrictions on Russian state securities and lending, transaction bans with listed state firms and the Central Bank of Russia, and limits on deposits, crypto and payment services for Russians. It applies directly to everyone in the EU and to EU nationals and companies, banks included. Banks must screen for these restrictions, refuse covered business, report large deposits and Central Bank of Russia assets, and keep non-EU subsidiaries from undermining the measures.

summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Council Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 as published in the Official Journal

text.en: The EU asset freeze on people and entities listed for undermining Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence, the core Russia listing regime. It applies directly to everyone in the EU and to EU nationals and companies, banks included. A bank must freeze the assets of anyone in its annex, never make funds available to them directly or indirectly, report frozen assets and unfrozen listed assets to its competent authority within two weeks, and use best efforts to keep entities it controls outside the EU from undermining the measures.

summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Council Regulation (EC) No 765/2006 as published in the Official Journal; title as amended, read in the consolidated text of 24 July 2026 (CELEX 02006R0765-20260724)

text.en: The EU sanctions against Belarus, for its internal situation and its involvement in Russia's war on Ukraine: an asset freeze on listed persons plus wide trade and financial restrictions. It applies directly to everyone in the EU and to EU nationals and companies, banks included. A bank must freeze listed assets and not make funds available, refuse dealings in covered Belarusian state securities, cap deposits from Belarusian persons and entities, not offer them crypto or certain payment services, report large deposits and pass compliance information to its authority.

summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Council Regulation (EU) No 267/2012 as published in the Official Journal

text.en: The EU sanctions against Iran over its nuclear programme: asset freezes, trade restrictions on sensitive goods and controls on financial dealings with Iran. It applies directly to everyone in the EU and to EU nationals and companies, banks included. A bank must freeze listed assets and not make funds available, transfer funds with Iranian banks only in permitted categories, notify its authority in advance of transfers with Iranian persons from EUR 10 000 and get prior authorisation where the amount or purpose requires it, and not open accounts or correspondent relationships with Iranian banks.

summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1509 as published in the Official Journal

text.en: The EU sanctions against North Korea (DPRK), giving effect to UN measures and adding EU ones: asset freezes, wide trade bans and a near-complete cut-off of financial links with the country. It applies directly to everyone in the EU and to EU nationals and companies, banks included. A bank must freeze listed assets and not make funds available, not transfer funds to or from North Korea outside narrow exceptions, and not open accounts, correspondent relationships or ownership links with North Korean banks, reporting relevant information to its authority.

summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Council Regulation (EC) No 2580/2001 as published in the Official Journal

text.en: The EU's own counter-terrorism sanctions list, giving effect to a UN Security Council resolution on terrorist financing, covering people, groups and entities the Council designates for involvement in terrorist acts. It applies directly to everyone in the EU and to EU nationals and companies, banks included. A bank must freeze the funds and economic resources of the listed persons and groups, must not make funds available to them directly or indirectly, and must report frozen accounts and other relevant information to its national competent authority.

A bank must not grant loans or other financing to entities in Crimea or Sevastopol, acquire participations there or provide related investment services, and must notify its authority before carrying out older contracts the Regulation still allows.

summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 as published in the Official Journal

text.en: The EU Blocking Statute protects EU businesses from foreign sanctions laws that reach beyond their own country, namely the third-country laws listed in its annex. It applies directly to EU companies and residents, banks included. A bank must not comply with those foreign laws or court requests based on them unless the Commission authorises it, and must inform the Commission within 30 days when such laws affect its economic or financial interests.

summaries.sourceLabel: EUR-Lex, Directive (EU) 2024/1226 as published in the Official Journal

text.en: Sets common minimum rules on which breaches of EU sanctions are crimes, such as making funds available to a listed person or failing to freeze assets, and on penalties for people and companies, and adds sanctions breaches to the predicate offences for money laundering. As a directive it binds the member states except Denmark, which does not take part, and not a bank directly; each bound country writes these offences into its criminal law. A bank has no duties of its own under the Directive; its sanctions duties come from the sanctions regulations.

summaries.sourceLabel: European Banking Authority, EBA/GL/2024/14 (Restrictive Measures Guidelines) guideline page

text.en: European Banking Authority guidelines on the governance, policies, procedures and controls financial institutions need to comply with EU and national sanctions. They are addressed to financial institutions and their supervisors, which apply them through supervision. In practice a bank's management body approves and oversees its sanctions strategy, a senior staff member owns the framework, and the bank assesses its exposure, keeps lists current, acts on matches without delay and trains staff.

summaries.sourceLabel: European Banking Authority, EBA/GL/2024/15 (Restrictive Measures Guidelines for PSPs and CASPs) guideline page

text.en: European Banking Authority guidelines on what payment and crypto-asset service providers, banks included, must do to apply sanctions when transferring funds and crypto-assets, focusing on know-your-customer checks, screening and due diligence. Supervisors apply them through supervision. In practice a bank calibrates and reviews its screening system, screens customers and every transfer and its parties, investigates matches promptly, suspends and freezes on a true match and reports to its authority.
